reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: An imprinting disorder of the chromosome 14q32.2 DLK1/MEG3 region in which the maternal contribution is lost, so paternally expressed genes are over-represented
The pregnancy is often complicated by marked polyhydramnios and a large placenta, prompting antenatal referral
The chest radiograph is the diagnostic clue: a small bell-shaped thorax with ribs that flare into a characteristic coat-hanger configuration
Neonates typically present with respiratory distress from thoracic constriction, and many require prolonged ventilatory support
Abdominal wall problems (omphalocele or diastasis recti) and feeding difficulty are common in the newborn period
It is the clinical mirror image of Temple syndrome, which arises from loss of the paternal contribution at the same locus (maternal uniparental disomy 14)
Later childhood may bring developmental delay, laryngomalacia, and a tendency to become overweight
Confirmation rests on methylation analysis of the 14q32.2 imprinted region, supported by microarray and uniparental disomy studies
reference.pathophysiology: The condition results from a disturbance of genomic imprinting at the DLK1/MEG3 domain on chromosome 14q32.2, a region controlled by differentially methylated regions that are normally set differently on the maternal and paternal chromosomes. When the maternally derived contribution is absent or silenced, whether through paternal uniparental disomy, a maternal deletion, or an epimutation, the paternally expressed genes such as DLK1 and RTL1 are over-dosed while the maternally expressed transcripts including MEG3 are lost. This imbalance in imprinted gene expression disrupts skeletal, placental, and neurological development, producing the thoracic dysplasia, abdominal wall defects, and neurodevelopmental features that define the phenotype. Because the same locus underlies Temple syndrome when the opposite parental contribution is affected, the two disorders behave as reciprocal imprinting conditions.
additionalDifferentials: Temple syndrome (maternal uniparental disomy 14), the reciprocal imprinting disorder
Prader-Willi syndrome and other neonatal hypotonia/imprinting disorders
Skeletal dysplasias with small thorax such as asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy
Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum when overgrowth and abdominal wall defects predominate
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia as a cause of neonatal respiratory failure
Trisomy 18 and other aneuploidies presenting with polyhydramnios and dysmorphism
additionalInvestigations: Methylation-specific analysis of the 14q32.2 imprinted region to confirm the imprinting defect
Chromosomal microarray to detect deletions or copy-number change at the locus
Uniparental disomy testing using informative microsatellite or SNP markers with parental samples
Chest radiography to demonstrate the bell-shaped thorax and coat-hanger rib pattern
Antenatal ultrasound assessment for polyhydramnios, thoracic size, and abdominal wall integrity
Neonatal respiratory and feeding assessment including consideration of laryngomalacia
redFlags: Severe neonatal respiratory distress from a constricted thorax requiring urgent airway and ventilatory support
Marked antenatal polyhydramnios raising the risk of preterm labour
Large abdominal wall defect needing prompt surgical planning
Failure to establish feeding with resultant faltering growth
reference.prognosis: Outlook is dominated by the neonatal respiratory compromise, which can be life-threatening in the most severely affected infants; those who survive the newborn period often show gradual improvement in respiratory mechanics as the chest grows, though developmental delay, feeding problems, and a later tendency to excess weight gain frequently persist and warrant long-term multidisciplinary follow-up.
pitfalls: Overlooking the coat-hanger rib sign on the neonatal chest film and attributing distress to other causes
Testing with karyotype or microarray alone, which can miss an imprinting defect that requires methylation analysis
Failing to counsel that recurrence risk differs markedly depending on the underlying molecular mechanism
Not recognising the reciprocal relationship with Temple syndrome when interpreting locus-specific results

management: Provide neonatal respiratory support with mechanical ventilation for thoracic constriction, anticipating prolonged weaning
Surgically repair abdominal wall defects such as omphalocele
Support nutrition with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding for feeding difficulty
Assess and manage upper-airway problems including laryngomalacia
Undertake developmental surveillance with early intervention for delay
Confirm the diagnosis by methylation-specific analysis of the 14q32.2 region and provide genetic counselling on recurrence risk
Coordinate multidisciplinary neonatology, respiratory, surgical and clinical genetics care
